newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK analysts fear bear market will mark handover.
newsitem.headline: HK analysts fear bear market will mark handover.

text.p: Recent market trends have forced local brokers and analysts to think the unthinkable -- that the Hong Kong stock market might be in a downswing at mid-year during the British colony's reversion to China.
"Hong Kong and the PRC (People's Republic of China) would hate to see the market in a slump at the handover," said Andrew To at OSK Asia Securities.
China regains sovereignty over Hong Kong after more than 150 years of British rule at midnight on June 30, and a bull market rally would be a celebratory scenario.
But a growing number of brokers and analysts have turned bearish in their assessment of the market's outlook for the coming three to nine months.

That view has nothing to do with politics and everything to do with interest rates and business cycles, and signs of strength like the market's sharp rally last Wednesday could be a bear trap ready to close around 13,000, they warned.
"We have taken out 12,500 and the next level will be 12,900. But I recommend a sell at that level," said analyst Ted Chen of Technical Data Inc.
The Hang Seng hit an all-time traded high of 14,004.93 on January 16. It later hit a traded low of 11,951.94 on April 1.

The index's 239-point surge on Wednesday fed optimism that the market may be shaking off the sluggishness that has been dogging it for the past two months. After a mixed performance over the next two days, the index ended at 12,541.18 on Friday, a gain of 24.58 points for the volatile week.
Wednesday's rally was in line with big jumps in U.S. stocks and bonds the previous day, investors nervously pouncing on any clue on interest rate trends.
"It is all interest rates and one has to be careful now. The U.S. market is looking overvalued and fragile," said Gary Wong, sales director at Vickers Ballas.
Markets have grown more volatile since the United States raised interest rates by 25 basis points in March, and pessimists say the hike confirmed a bear market trend.

"A global equity bear market has begun, triggered by the sell signal given for U.S. bonds when the 30-year (U.S. Treasury bond) rose through the critical level of 6.90 percent," said technical analyst John Schofield of NAVA SC Securities.
The long bond yield hit a low around 6.3 percent at the end of November, then surged to the critical level of 6.9 in late January. It ended at 7.07 percent in New York on Thursday.
Technical analysts such as Schofield worry the long bond's chart signals weakness in the U.S. and Hong Kong equity markets.
"I am not ultra bearish, but we look like we're facing a six- to nine-month bear market in the blue chips," said Schofield.
Fundamental analysts are also worried about the bond yield and interest rate trends.

"The Hong Kong market is selling purely at fair value now in an environment where we are looking for one or two rate hikes by the U.S.," Ajay Kapur, regional strategist at UBS Securities, told Reuters Financial Television.
But the current cloudy outlook was no reason to despair on Hong Kong, analysts said. In two to three months, if the market drops another 10 percent, it would be a buy, Kapur said.
And many analysts still expect the market to end the year at higher, even record levels despite bumps along the way.
Merrill Lynch recently said the Hang Seng could reach 15,000 by year end, although range-bound trading was likely over the next couple of months as local property prices corrected.

"With potentially two more (interest) rate hikes in the pipeline, we sense that foreign investors approaching the last investment lap before the July 1 sovereignty change have found the perfect excuse to sit tight," it said.
